en: Having paid homage to the supreme Victor Mahāvīra, who has worn away old age and death, I shall speak fifty-six verses suitable for the learned. (Chapp.
1) [The first verse: A man who is truly prosperous yet appears as if poor, and who is content despite his state...
The thoughts of one whose mind is fixed on the dharma of self-restraint become auspicious, even when they appear inauspicious. (Chapp.
2) Just as planets in the sky, dreams in sleep, or omens at the edge of the forest portend for a man according to his past karmas, so too do these [thoughts] foretell his fate. (Chapp. 3)
For one who carries the Jina in his heart—the abode of auspiciousness for the three worlds—all dreams are praised, all omens are favorable, and all constellations are auspicious. (Chapp.
4) In some places gold is not valued, and in others there is the wretchedness of begging.
A person whose nature is not straightforward does not receive honor.
(Chapp. 5) The sun burns from afar; fire burns when touched by the limbs;
separation from a beloved burns; and even a virtuous friend burns when out of sight. (Chapp. 6)

Separation from loved ones burns; poverty burns; slander by others burns; and a deed done later [when it is too late] burns. The suffering born from the destruction of virtuous qualities and the arising of non-existent faults [is likewise burning]. (Chapp. 7)
It dries up even the ocean—how much more so the hearts of men? (Chapp.
8) What is the use of speaking of another’s faults, whether they be true or false?
No wealth or fame is gained; one merely becomes a source of sorrow for one’s friends. (Chapp. 9)
Conquer bitterness with sweetness, pride with forbearance, greed with contentment, and quarreling by remaining silent.
Be satisfied with what you have done yourself, until your own misdeeds pass away. (Chapp. 10)
Even while he was still in his physical body, it was not possible to do what was pleasing to him day after day.
How indeed could one contemplate evil toward him, who has now arrived free from anger, with hands as delicate as lotus petals, having dwelt in my house? (Chapp. 11–12)
To virtuous people, the mental suffering arising from the death of a dear guest who has not yet been fully satisfied is even greater than [the grief over] their own death. (Chapp.
13) Indeed, one does not eat too much; as it is filled, so it becomes a source of happiness.
Even one who has gone to the fifth hell does not become a dear guest [of Yama] for five days. (Chapp.
14) Blessed are those who, though they know the Dharma well, thoroughly practice it;
for the essence of life is insubstantial—all things change in an instant. (Chapp. 15)
She is my mother, he is my father, he is my friend, my kinsman, and my very glory—he who provides the path and method for the Dharma that brings about complete and ultimate welfare.
Neither mother, nor father, nor son, nor any circle of kinsmen can do that. (Chapp. 16)
Whatever righteous conduct the noble ones perform when teaching the Dharma—why do you remain so confident? The days pass away like travelers on horseback;
they do not take you into account, nor are you taken into account by them. (Chapp. 17–18)
The people were delighted, thinking, "A festival for Indra has arrived; it is delightful!
But those poor fools did not realize that the year’s tally had been cast down! [Chapp.
19] One who sits on a high seat, who is full of great desire, and who issues commands without courtesy—

One who is lazy, fond of sleep, and prone to anger does not remain beloved for long. (Chapp. 20) Those who suddenly show affection, speak whatever comes to mind when pressed, and embrace one by the side, attain the state of being beloved through their lack of self-control. (Chapp. 21)
Even a stranger becomes dear when he acts agreeably, speaks with courtesy, utters pleasant words, and follows one's will. (Chapp.
22) He who conforms to another’s will heals their wounds and reveals their virtues.

Indeed, it is not only for humans, but even for gods, that [this] is difficult to obtain. // Chapp.23 A wise man should say both "it will come" and "it will be so"; thus the other person becomes satisfied, and the other [result] is likewise exactly the same. // Chapp.24
The graceful conduct of a master is honored; the pride of a beloved woman is [honored];
the speech of one who is capable and wise is [honored]; and silence is [honored] by one who does not know. // Chapp.
25 He does not endure harshness; he does not speak bitter words; he does not find fault; he reveals virtues.
The good person, a great warrior of courtesy, does not become angry even when others are angry. (Chapp.
26) The good person does not become angry at all; if he does become angry, he does not think of anything inauspicious;
if he thinks of something, he does not speak of it; and if he speaks, he remains ashamed. (Chapp. 27)
That which a virtuous person endures out of shame, the shameless person knows well; therefore, know that it is the incompetent one who endures this.
He does not recognize what is being entreated, and even when something pleasant is said, he speaks what is unpleasant.
It is not accomplished by giving; indeed, there is no remedy for a wicked person.
Poison is bound with mantras, an elephant with ropes, and water with embankments;
but we know of no bond for a wicked person whose nature is poison.
This is the nature of everyone: when something pleasant arises, one acts to make it more pleasant.
But the nature of a true friend is such that they act to bring about what is pleasant, even when no pleasure has been requested. (Chapp.
31) When a task arises, one should diligently attend to a wicked person.
Poison, it is said, arises from ambrosia; poison does not arise from poison itself. (Chapp.

32) Even if forbearance is disregarded, and even if there is no respect for one who practices forbearance, nevertheless forbearance must be practiced; there is no kinsman equal to forbearance. (Chapp. 33)
How can one be angry with him to whom one must again offer salutation?
How is it even possible to be angry with one who is utterly devoid of virtue?
Forbearance is the punishment for anger, and the restraint of the qualities of desire is the punishment [for them].

Avoidance of wicked people who are intent on quarreling is the punishment [for the wise]. (Chapp. 35) Blessed are those masters of learning who, though they have committed offenses and harbor enmity, remain affectionate toward those who prostrate before them, and whose anger is fierce for only a moment. (Chapp. 36)
One must always be wary of the speech of wicked people, which is as terrifying as a torrent of excellent jewels falling from a mountain when its tongue has been turned upside down.
Even if one speaks spontaneously, manifesting the truth of the entire world, it is uttered without reflection. (Chapp. 37)
That human vampire wanders even upon the earth, full of suspicion. (Chapp.
38) One who is neutral becomes attached in an instant; being attached, he becomes dispassionate in an instant.
One who was neutral, as soon as he becomes dispassionate, roams from house to house proclaiming faults. (Chapp. 39)
A true friend is won over after a long time; once he is won over, he remains so for a long time even if he is alienated.
Even if a true friend should become alienated, he does not reveal one's faults. (Chapp.
40) He who acts with gentle guile makes up for what is deficient, fills what is empty, and brings forth gold.
The words of the truly virtuous are not called "wives" [to be kept secret], for they are vessels of noble wisdom. (Chapp.
41) Eat that which is digestible; speak that which is fit for the great assembly. The truly virtuous speak that which does not transgress the proper time. (Chapp. 42)
Speak only as much as is necessary; abandon that which is useless for one who speaks only what is necessary.
Cast off that burden which you do not lay down halfway along the path. Indeed, burdens are called "burdens" only when they are carried by those who shrink from them. (Chapp. 43)
The burden of moral conduct must be carried by you for as long as life lasts, without rest. (Chapp.
44) He who does not know Sanskrit and cannot even speak well-purified Prakrit—silence is his refuge, or else [withdrawal] from the assembly. (Chapp. 45)
One who has not studied at all, one who has studied only half, or one who has studied poorly yet utters the speech of the wise—that person is equal to a donkey. (Chapp.
46) Who produces the fragrance of blue lotuses and the sweetness of sugarcane?
Do you follow the grace of excellent elephants and the discipline of those born of noble lineage? (Chapp.
47) Attend to them, speak what is pleasing, and understand with your heart whatever task must be done: the peacock speaks sweetly, yet it swallows the venomous serpent. (Chapp. 48)
Sugar-cane is sweet, the moon is beautiful, sandalwood is indeed most fragrant, and one who is well-born is noble; what fault is there in such conduct?
[But] he who speaks with words made of molasses while his heart is made of poison—[that is the fault]. (Chapp. 49)
Therefore, one must avoid such a person with great care, like a snake in a grain-bin. (Chapp.
50) Even when a wicked person is not seen, there is apprehension at the mere mention of his name;
even when he speaks a lie, who does not fear him, crying out, "A snake! A snake!"? (Chapp. 51)
The old man, trembling from the cold as he rose up upon seeing the prince, wept on the path, remembering his own youth;
for the intellect of an old man is perverted, yet that very intellect of an old man returns when it is restrained. // Chapp. 52 //
Time does not look upon the head turning white with such strength. (Chapp.
53) It is that same body, those same moments, and those same eyes;
it is as if fate does not spare the head, for old age has bestowed its curse. (Chapp. 54)
"O Lord, that very house which was shown to me by my eyes with great affection—now that it has been driven out by old age, here it remains, rejected.
Thus, with his body supported by a staff, his youth gone, he remains content in this very state. (Chapp. 55)
Even when spoken to harshly, he endured it, saying: "You have gone; it is time for you to be angry! (Chapp.
56) The head is grey, the face is full of wrinkles; old age has set in—alas, death is now beyond thought! O living being, practice righteousness; take refuge in the Name. (Chapp. 57)
Abandon a woman who is bitter of speech; abandon a friend in whom there is no sincerity; abandon a master who does not give; and abandon a residence where one is treated with contempt. (Chapp.
58) He becomes angry even at what is spoken kindly; he utters his words only after knitting his brows.
Ancient karma drives a man through the deception of women. (Chapp.
59) This is the nature of women: they cause everyone else to feel dejection, yet they do not cause it for the one who is fully capable of enjoying their company. (Chapp. 60)

In this world, those sages who have not yet enjoyed the company of beloved ones, who adopted the ascetic life while still children, and who have never experienced separation from their loved ones, live happily. (Chapp.
61) Dwelling in celestial palaces is easily obtained, and the earth under a single umbrella is also easy to attain.
In this world, however, the feet of the Jina Vardhamāna are exceedingly rare.
// Chapp.62 Sugar-cane is sweet by nature, while the neem tree is bitter; fire is burning.
Such is the difference in the innate disposition between the virtuous and the wicked, established by their very nature. // Chapp.63
What need is there for the path of weapons when [the enemy] can be cut down by a lotus leaf? When one should speak sweetly, what is the use of speaking bitter words? (Chapp.
64) Those who have gone abroad after being comforted with sweet words...
Remembering those [past pleasures], they do not fix their affection elsewhere. (Chapp.
65) Those who have been rebuked with harsh words and whose bonds of affection have been severed, remembering those [past pleasures], depart from there for another place. (Chapp. 66)
The tongue of the virtuous speaks what is beneficial, moderate, and graspable; it speaks according to place and time, is not opposed to the next world, and is aimed at attaining excellence.
This [tongue] withstands the blows of weapons, the blows of whips, and the blows of force.

The tongue of the ill-behaved person longs to cause [others] to be burned. // Chapp.68 A good person who forms a friendship with a wicked person, having taken him for a "good man," is like a treasure found through great effort that later fails to fulfill one's expectations. // Chapp.69
Through association with the wicked, which is as sweet as a piece of sugarcane in its onset, it becomes undesirable in the end, like poison swallowed unknowingly. // Chapp.
70 Even if gold were to be produced from mountains, and pearls from elephants...
Modesty is the mark of the well-born; what fault is there in practicing it? (Chapp.
71) A good person should endure the wicked one who is capable of giving a retort:
a crow does not take away the glory of a bull simply by perching upon its back. (Chapp. 72)
There is only one fault that is reckoned as being beyond remedy for a woman adorned with every ornament: that she is regarded by wicked people as a mere man. (Chapp.
73) Those three who have never before been seen in the royal court, in the family of a teacher, or among courtesans—
Those who possess knowledge, pride, and cleverness are outsiders [to true liberation]. (Chapp.
74) Having acquired knowledge, having performed heroic deeds in battle, and having even scaled Mount Meru—without merit, from where can happiness come? (Chapp. 75)
Even a tiny great medicine, when administered at the right time, brings one back to life;

but what is the use of mango juice to the dead, even if it is mixed with the essence of nectar? Bathing for one who has already bathed, and chewing betel for one who has already eaten—whatever that may be—is likewise useless. (Chapp. 76)
A verse recited at the right moment, the three of these distinguish one another as leading to heaven.

// Chapp.77 A wife who is well-born, who has found her opportunity, who is skilled in her craft, who is endowed with wealth, and who is devoted to her husband—these three distinguish themselves as the thorn [of a household]. // Chapp.78
Speech delivered at the proper time is beautiful; speech delivered at the proper time brings happiness.
But speech delivered at the wrong time destroys even that which has already been accomplished. (Chapp.
79) Why do you flee from me? For there is no refuge in the entire three worlds.
Setting aside the words of the Lord of Jinas, everything else is mere clamor. // Chapp.
80 A good person is by nature straightforward; even when rubbed by wicked people, like a mirror with ash, they become even more pure. // Chapp. 81
When a good person is provoked by a wicked one and addressed with harsh words, his anger wanders externally like a bee hovering around a closed lotus bud. (Chapp.
82) Just as he is further pursued, so too, through the fault of his own lowliness...
A wicked person climbs onto the head like dust from a spinning wheel; of this there is no doubt. (Chapp.
83) He without whom one cannot live is entreated even if he has committed an offense:
tell me, when a city fire breaks out, who does not hold fire dear? (Chapp. 84)
The virtuous speak of him and place him at their very head;
he is like the ocean that does not overstep its shore even at the appointed time. (Chapp.
85) One whose mind is overcome by the power of others, who is immoral, a speaker of falsehood, and fickle—
Where people are not seen, even that very forest is delightful. (Chapp.
86) Whatever is one's own inherent nature remains exactly so even in the company of the virtuous; an arrow, though fixed upon a bowstring and drawn by its qualities, still kills. (Chapp. 87)
Avoiding the company of the wicked, behold the fruit obtained by sesame:
that it attained the head of the Lord, fragrant with the scent of Madanāhī. (Chapp.
88) By those very [beings] were they raised up, and through whose favor their majesty increased.
Fires burn Mount Vindhya; indeed, association with the wicked is destruction itself. (Chapp.
89) The sound of the anklets of virtuous women is a delight to the ear;
yet that very same sound is harsh to the ears of those bound in fetters and consumed by malice. (Chapp. 90)
The forest is blocked by elephants, the grove by monkeys, the royal palace by slanderers, and the water by crocodiles; O fickle Fate, where has the good man gone? (Chapp.
91) As we wander throughout the entire circle of the earth, there is no such house of a king to be found.
Where three or four wicked men, provoked for no reason, are not seen. (Chapp.

92) Just as a lapidary creates flaws even in gems that are utterly pure, highly valuable, and heavy with essence, so too does the company of the wicked create defects even in [the best of] jewels. (Chapp. 93)
In those very same rivers where thirsty bulls go down to drink water,
they destroy the banks with their horns.
In a similar human birth, the wicked man causes torment while the virtuous person brings comfort.
Iron armor alone protects life, while the sword takes it away. // Chapp.

95 With the water of moonlight, the moon washes away the stains from the faces of the quarters—the brides of the directions—but he does not wash away his own stain; everyone is deluded regarding their own affairs. // Chapp. 96
Whatever is dear to someone, that person establishes them in a beautiful nature:
a tigress considers her cub to be auspicious and gentle. // Chapp.
97 The passionate, the hateful, the deluded, and the one previously seized by false views—these four...
[Such people] are unworthy of instruction; one who is balanced [in mind], however, is worthy. // Chapp.
98 Everyone sees the tiny holes on the tips of others' hairs, yet they do not see their own faults, even those as large as the peaks of Mount Himavat. // Chapp. 99
Those who are attached perceive virtues; those who are dispassionate perceive faults;
but those who stand in the middle perceive both faults and virtues.
Like the streak of gold on a heap of stones when rubbed against other elephants, [the true nature of things is revealed].
The true essence of those of noble birth is revealed in the crucible of adversity. (Chapp.
101) It is fitting that one should love with a heart composed of sincerity and affection;
however, people laugh at one who gives their heart to someone who has no heart. (Chapp. 102)
Those who are honored for their virtues, yet remain unrecognized even when they have cast off all affection— even for them, O son, weeping is due in this Kali age.
We do not know how virtues can be cultivated among people whose nature is so fickle.
Even though the rays of the moon are cold as snow, the lotus does not desire them. // Chapp.
104 Pure conduct, honest dealings, true nature, dignity, and patience—all these crumble due to the fault of the power of this Kali age, even among kinsmen. // Chapp. 105
Kāliya was told by Kṛṣṇa regarding the jewel on his hood: "A Ā A Ā A Ā!
Even the poisons produced from one's own body recede when the gods are summoned.
Who indeed has not encountered suffering? Or tell me, for whom is happiness eternal?
To whom does constant devotion belong? To whom does unerring good fortune belong? (Chapp.
107) Everyone experiences the ripening of the fruits of their own previously committed karmas; others become merely instrumental causes regarding both faults and virtues. (Chapp. 108)
Even for the nine types of excellent men who strive, no matter what state may arise that is not pleasing to fate, it does not come about if it cannot be reached through thought.
Otherwise, it is contemplated with a heart straight as an arrow, full of joy.
By the power of fate, even the commencement of an undertaking turns out quite otherwise. (Chapp.
110) Everyone, though led astray by fate, says, "It was the eighth moon";
but when the moon was seized by Rāhu, who was the eighth one then? (Chapp. 111)
Mounted upon his excellent chariot in the vast expanse of the sky,
he is difficult to behold; it is heard that even the peak of the setting sun is hard to reach compared to him.
When a thing is transformed according to its specific method, even the sun is swallowed by Rāhu; likewise, even the bow that shatters the world is brought to rest. (Chapp. 112)
O King, look at this wretch standing beneath the *vabbula* tree; even for a god, such a state as this is not fit to be swallowed.
What kind of fate can do anything? What can be squeezed out [of it]? (Chapp.
113) Fortune is the gold of the three worlds; even for him, it is given by Hara as a mere trifle. Śaṅkara is made naked by that very fortune. (Chapp. 114)
"O Lord of the World, you who are said to destroy even what is hidden, even so, you have broken Hara’s bow and cast off his bones from your neck.
Others say that Janardana was the third brother of Hara.
Even for him, sleep was ordained by fate at the wrong time. (Chapp.
116) Only what is ordained by destiny is obtained: nectar was for the gods, though Lakṣmī dwells even in the ocean;
yet for Śiva, though he is the brother of [Viṣṇu], poison arose. (Chapp. 117)
The world is ensnared by the power of destiny; who is the protector of the three-eyed one?
Even the bull of Hara grazes on grass, and Vāsuki feeds only on air.
(Chappan 118) Even though the three-eyed one alone [rules] upon the earth...
He is saluted by hosts of gods; even so, O wretch, how can he be bowed to by you,
whose head has sought refuge in him?
Taking the head, it is swallowed by Rāhu. // Chapp.
119 // For one dwelling in the midst of matted locks, whence can there be an expansion of virtues? Of the moon of Śiva, that portion alone remains which has not yet waned. // Chapp. 120 //

Even those devoid of virtues gain respect among the virtuous because of their wealth, for it is by means of this that men are called "kūya-saras" (well-voices), just as even wells are called "kūya-saras" (well-voices) because of their reeds.
Just as a mouse has both hands occupied with a single grain of rice... [Chapp. 121]
Likewise, those who do not recognize excellence become arrogant even over a trifle. Know that the virtues of the virtuous remain manifest and of great value;
it is like cowherds searching for a precious gem in a heap of curd.
The wisdom of even those who do not speak is known through the deeds of the virtuous;
do jewels have to speak in order to be grasped by the thousands? (Chapp. 124) O Ā!
O Ā! O Ā! O Ā! Even for the worthless, there are eight states according to their desire. (Chapp. 124)
Virtues, which are praiseworthy by the virtuous, are acquired through pleasures. // Chapp.
125 A man who has performed unwholesome karma in the past, though striving for the wholesome, falls, tripped up by the unwholesome, into the snare of strife, quarrel, and affliction. // Chapp. 126
Even in the thick darkness of night, the calf seeks out its mother;
the heart knows the beloved, and the eyes recognize the dress. (Chapp.
127) He whose thousands of virtues people do not describe in the assemblies of the virtuous—
Of what use is that birth which serves merely to destroy the youth of one's mother? (Chapp.
128) Do not seize upon only the faults, and praise only the rare virtues of people:
even though the ocean is full of salt, it is called the "Treasure-Mine of Jewels" in the world. (Chapp. 129)
Everyone is fond of virtues; who would honor a person devoid of virtues? Believe me, even bees do not frequent a flower that lacks fragrance. (Chapp.
130) [The tree of the Dharma] has its roots bound by a net of virtues, bears the fruit of truth, and possesses sprouts of right knowledge.
Who would not rest under the tree of a friend—a kinsman not made of flesh and blood? (Chapp.
131) Who does not remember the happiness of friendship—characterized by genuine affection, the endurance of shared suffering, excellent conduct, and laughter seen from afar? (Chapp. 132)

What is the use of life for one who has not even a single friend—a friend who is a treasury of secrets, a place of rest for recounting joys and sorrows? (Chapp. 133) One should cultivate that kind of friendship which remains steadfast when misfortune strikes or when traveling through a foreign land.
Like a painted mural on a wall, he does not turn his back [on you].

O good friend, you who are bound by affection, dear to your kinsmen, and skilled in discerning your own interests—though you have been made into such a state, avoid this kind of friend. (Chapp. 134–135)
Even by the moon standing in the mid-heavens, it is not possible to bring joy to the cakora birds;
their alternating separation and union, they perform once again as friends alone. // Chapp.
136 // Just as when it is full of sap, so too when dry, Mount Vindhya maintains its daily [growth].

The great do not relax their efforts toward one who has grown up in their lap, even if that person is devoid of virtue. (Chapp. 137) One should seek the company of superior persons even if it proves fruitless;
for even a blade of grass attached to the side of Mount Meru becomes gold. (Chapp. 138)
O great tree, do not worry; my life-root has perished.
In the darkness of night, where can the birds find shelter in the ruined grove?
O full moon, fill the interiors of the worlds with the water of your moonlight!
Who knows how long this unstable prosperity of yours will last? (Chapp.
140) While those seeking wealth give it away, what is the use of testing the recipient? Does the cloud, while raining, distinguish between the level and the uneven ground? (Chapp. 141)
Having observed the binding of the *bali* offering, a man should perform an examination of the vessel; for one who gives to the unvirtuous does not avoid falling into ruin. (Chapp.
142) Give, and do not fear; this [vessel] is fashioned from most precious jewels.
Just as a vessel for Śrī (Lakṣmī) and a vessel for misfortune pass by in turn, so it is. // Chapp.
143 A certain man becomes possessed of vast prosperity by giving incessantly;
another, though constantly wandering about, remains forever destitute. // Chapp. 144
When wealth is stolen by kings, fire, or thieves, one speaks of "lakhs" and "thousands";

yet when it has been lost to another, because one has requested it back, there is poverty and the taking of gifts. Even a small amount of that prosperity is counted as such when it is common to the entire world. (Chapp. 145)
Water is drunk even when poured out, yet not even a drop of the ocean is consumed. (Chapp.
146) That same amount of water belongs to the sea; that is its supreme vastness.
There is not even a single *pala* of it that can quench thirst. (Chapp. 147)
It is not eaten, it is not drunk,
and it is not given to the helpless; such is the nature of the dhattūra poison.
...until they become wicked.
// Chapp.148 Exhausted by the weariness of being passed from hand to hand in the process of begging, those who dwell in the houses of misers lie down as if they were dead. // Chapp.149
At that time, with every effort, the miserly ones diligently protected their wealth with loud shouts of "thut-thuk," like a maiden who has been stolen by another.
Thus, the prosperity in the houses of the misers remained suppressed, accompanied by those cries of "thut-thuk. (Chapp. 150)
Even though he has been married by the elder brother, he enjoys [the company] of others. (Chapp.

151) The head is covered with grey hair, the space between the breasts has sagged, the teeth have fallen out from the mouth, and both hands tremble; yet the mind still maintains its youth. (Chapp. 152)
With eyebrows knitted in deep concern, asking about every detail at every step, the elders search the surface of the earth for their lost youth;
yet that which has perished cannot be recovered even by others. (Chappannaya 153)
"Give! Give!"—thus one's limbs are wasted away;
placing one's hands upon the ground, one rises up;
yet even so, the Dharma is not practiced day by day. (Chapp. 154)
O Illustrious One, each single step you take is established like a fire;
O guest of youth, old age will shatter your pride.
For those fortunate ones, O Greatly Renowned One, who have fallen forever into the ocean of saṃsāra— (Chapp. 155)
"O Lord, you are the navigator for those submerged in the waters of misfortune. (Chapp.
156) Whoever reads this treasury of verses composed by the learned in this world shall attain vast prosperity and find good fortune among the people. (Chapp. 157)

[Supplement] Devotion to the teaching of the Jina, fellowship with the learned, association with the distinguished, and a commitment to giving to the best of sages—these do not arise from meager merits. (Chapp. 158)

This young bee does not merely protect the lotus grove; by some quality of skillfulness, he nourishes himself and drinks the nectar. (Chapp. 159) That by which one is shamed among people, and that by which one's own family tradition is defiled—
O Sundara, even though life remains in the throat, do not commit that [evil deed]. (Chapp.
160) Human existence has health as its essence; the Dharma has truth as its essence; knowledge has certainty as its essence; and happinesses have contentment as their essence. (Chapp. 161)
When a guest has arrived, what can a poor man do, even if he hurries?

That wretched blind man remains blind despite having his eyes rubbed with ointment. (Chapp. 162) Those who are true friends are those by whom no service whatsoever is neglected for one who has come to their house.
Those who constantly speak with smiles offer their own heads and seats [to others]. (Chapp.
163) Indeed, without the Dharma, even those who desire what is beneficial for their hearts wander like dogs;
like crows and cranes, such base men, greedy for the food of others, gnaw at them like woodworms. (Chapp. 164)
